title: Mastermind
description: Midnights closes with a confession disguised as a chess match: Swift admits the romance was never fate or luck — she quietly planned every move, then dares her lover to love her anyway.

pops.text: Track 13 — the finale of the standard edition of Midnights, Swift's tenth studio album, released October 21, 2022.
Swift wrote and produced the song with Jack Antonoff, her longtime collaborator, who co-wrote much of Midnights.
The song was partly inspired by the 2017 film Phantom Thread, whose controlling, calculating romance helped spark the lyric.
Nothing here is framed as chance: the narrator lists dominoes, checkers and masterminds as she admits she laid the groundwork.
Swift announced Midnights at the 2022 MTV Video Music Awards, accepting Video of the Year before revealing the album existed.
Midnights is built as a concept record about sleepless nights — 13 of them, one per track on the standard edition.
The official lyric video landed on Swift's YouTube channel on October 22, 2022, the day after the album dropped.
Swift performed 'Mastermind' on the Eras Tour, staging the song's chess imagery as a giant onstage board game.
Critics singled out the closer's twist: the schemer expects rejection, but her partner says he knew all along.
Antonoff and Swift first worked together on her 1989 album in 2014; by Midnights they were a decade into their partnership.

title: Golgi Apparatus
description: Phish's schoolboy biology joke turned forever anthem — a microscope, a ticket stub and four and a half minutes of pure bounce from their debut album Junta, in the official studio audio.

pops.text: It's track four on Junta, Phish's debut studio album — self-released on cassette in May 1989, years before the band had a record deal.
The title is literal school biology: the Golgi apparatus is the organelle inside cells that modifies and packages proteins — spotted here, quite correctly, through a microscope.
Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall wrote it with classmates Aaron Woolf and Szuter in eighth-grade science class at Princeton Day School.
Woolf's co-write ambushed him years later: at a party in California he heard the song, cried 'I wrote this!' — and was corrected: 'No, man, this is Phish.'
Junta was recorded at Euphoria Sound Studio in Revere, Massachusetts, with engineer Gordon Hookailo, and produced by the band itself.
It was already a stage veteran by then: the first known live performance came on October 12, 1986, at Goddard College in Vermont.
Elektra Records reissued Junta on CD in 1992 — and the little self-made album eventually went gold in 1997 and platinum in 2004.
The closing shout — 'I saw you with a ticket stub in your hand!' — became one of the most reliably roared-along lines at any Phish show.
Unlike the band's sprawling early epics, this one never wanders off: the studio cut runs about four and a half minutes, and live versions stay close to the script.
Woolf grew up to be a documentary filmmaker — his film King Corn won a Peabody Award — and in 2014 he ran for Congress in New York.

title: Finest Worksong
description: Document opens like a factory whistle: a muscular, horn-kicked call to seize the time that R.E.M. placed first on the album that finally carried them from college radio to the mainstream.

pops.text: 'Finest Worksong' is the opening track of Document, R.E.M.'s fifth album — its full title is even styled 'Document (R.E.M. No. 5)'.
Document, released in 1987, was the band's first album with producer Scott Litt, who would work with them for a decade.
It was issued as the album's third single, after 'The One I Love' and 'It's the End of the World as We Know It (And I Feel Fine)'.
All four members — Berry, Buck, Mills and Stipe — share the songwriting credit, as on nearly every R.E.M. song.
The album was recorded at Sound Emporium Studios in Nashville, Tennessee.
Document became R.E.M.'s breakthrough: their first Top 10 album in the US and their first to go platinum.
Michael Stipe's lyric mixes work slogans with self-improvement mantras — 'take your instinct by the reins' — half sermon, half satire.
The single version and its remixes stretched the song out; a 'Lengthy Club Mix' circulated for dancefloors.
The track sets the album's tone of political unease that runs through 'Welcome to the Occupation' and 'Exile in Oregon'.
R.E.M. kept it in live sets for years, including a storming performance at Glastonbury Festival in 1999.

title: Brown Sugar
description: Sticky Fingers opens with the Stones at full swagger — a Muscle Shoals-recorded riff monster that topped the US chart in 1971 and became so contested that the band eventually retired it live.

pops.text: Mick Jagger wrote the song in 1969 in Australia, in a burst of stream-of-consciousness while filming the movie Ned Kelly.
The released version was recorded in December 1969 at Muscle Shoals Sound Studio in Alabama, in a whirlwind session that also produced 'Wild Horses'.
It was the first single ever released on the band's own Rolling Stones Records label.
Released in April 1971, it hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and opened the Sticky Fingers album.
Saxophonist Bobby Keys delivers the honking solo — Keys was a fixture of the Stones' early-70s sound.
An alternate take with Eric Clapton on slide guitar, cut in London in 1970, stayed in the vaults until the 2015 Sticky Fingers deluxe reissue.
Sticky Fingers was the first full Stones album with guitarist Mick Taylor, and its famous zipper cover was conceived by Andy Warhol.
Producer Jimmy Miller, who helmed every Stones album from Beggars Banquet to Goats Head Soup, ran the sessions.
For decades it was a guaranteed concert staple, usually played near the end of the night.
In 2021 the Stones dropped it from their setlists, with Jagger acknowledging the lyric's slavery-era imagery no longer sat comfortably — it has stayed retired since.

title: Airplane
description: Michael Houser's signature song from Ain't Life Grand rides a pilot's daydream — take off, look down, leave it all below — and became so tied to Houser that the band grounded it for years after his death.

pops.text: 'Airplane' comes from Ain't Life Grand, Widespread Panic's fourth studio album, released in 1994.
Guitarist Michael 'Mikey' Houser wrote the song and sings lead — it became his signature tune.
The band debuted it live on March 2, 1994, at Saratoga Winners in Cohoes, New York.
A 1994 music video for the song was re-released by the band in 2021 as part of an archival video series.
The album was produced by John Keane, the Athens, Georgia studio owner who produced most of the band's records.
Houser co-founded the band in Athens in the mid-1980s and gave it its anxious name — from his own panic attacks, by band lore.
After Houser died of pancreatic cancer in August 2002, the song felt untouchable to his bandmates.
Panic shelved 'Airplane' for over four years, finally bringing it back on October 30, 2006.
With Jimmy Herring on lead guitar after 2006, the song returned to regular rotation as a tribute in all but name.
Fans still treat its opening notes as a Houser moment — one of the most emotional sing-alongs in the Panic catalog.

title: Sunrise
description: Norah Jones opens Feels Like Home by refusing to get out of bed — a feather-light love song co-written with bassist Lee Alexander that won a Grammy and fronted a million-selling first week.

pops.text: 'Sunrise' opens Feels Like Home, Norah Jones's second album, and was its lead single, released January 12, 2004 on Blue Note Records.
Jones co-wrote it with Lee Alexander, her bassist and bandleader — the pair anchored her band and later played together in the country side project the Little Willies.
The lyric is a lie-in manifesto: 'the clock's held 9:15 for hours,' and the afternoon has 'already come and gone' — morning never stood a chance against love.
Where her debut leaned toward jazz, Feels Like Home tilts country and folk — this is Jones settling into a rootsier, front-porch groove.
Jones produced the album with Arif Mardin, the veteran producer behind her debut — continuity in the studio while the songs themselves stretched out.
The album detonated commercially: Feels Like Home sold 1,022,000 copies in its first week in the US, the biggest opening week for any album since 2001.
It spent six weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, topped the charts in at least 16 countries, and finished as the second-best-selling album of 2004 in the US.
On mainstream pop radio it stayed a whisper — its real kingdom was adult-alternative radio, where 'Sunrise' climbed all the way to No. 1.
It was a traveler, too: the single reached No. 1 in Croatia and No. 4 in Canada — a very quiet song with a very long passport.
At the 2005 Grammy Awards it won Best Female Pop Vocal Performance — one of three awards Jones took home that night, including Record of the Year for her Ray Charles duet.

title: Hazy Shade of Winter
description: The Bangles took a folk-rock Simon & Garfunkel single they'd been covering onstage for years, cranked it into hard rock for the Less Than Zero soundtrack, and rode it to No. 2 in America.

pops.text: Paul Simon wrote the song; Simon & Garfunkel released the original as a single in October 1966 and later put it on Bookends (1968).
The Bangles had been performing the song live as early as March 1983, years before they were asked to record it.
They cut it for the soundtrack of the 1987 film Less Than Zero, starring Robert Downey Jr.
Their version drops the 'A' — it's billed simply as 'Hazy Shade of Winter'.
Released in late 1987, the single climbed to No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 in early 1988.
The video was the first directed by Jim Shea, later a major country-music video director.
The clip intercuts the band performing amid walls of TV screens with scenes from Less Than Zero.
It never appeared on a Bangles studio album — fans first got it on an album with their 1990 Greatest Hits.
The harder, guitar-driven arrangement fit the band's roots: they started in LA's Paisley Underground scene as the Bangs.
All four Bangles share the vocal attack, a group-harmony roar quite unlike the duo delicacy of the original.

title: Hunger Strike
description: A tribute record for a lost friend became grunge's founding duet: Chris Cornell, stuck on the low verses, watched an unknown Eddie Vedder walk to the mic and finish the song's other half.

pops.text: Temple of the Dog was Chris Cornell's tribute to his roommate Andrew Wood, the Mother Love Bone singer who died in March 1990.
'Hunger Strike' was the first single from the band's only album, released in January 1991.
Cornell wrote it, but struggled with the low verses in the studio — Eddie Vedder, newly arrived in Seattle, stepped in and sang them.
It was the first song Vedder recorded with the group; his harmonies turned a solo vocal into the famous duet.
The band mixed Soundgarden and future Pearl Jam members: Stone Gossard, Jeff Ament, Mike McCready and Matt Cameron.
The album was recorded in just 15 days at London Bridge Studio in Seattle with producer Rick Parashar.
The band's name comes from a lyric in Wood's Mother Love Bone song 'Man of Golden Words' — 'temple of the dog'.
A&M only pushed the album in 1992, once Soundgarden and Pearl Jam broke — then the song hit No. 4 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart and No. 7 on Alternative.
Director Paul Rachman shot the video at Seattle's Discovery Park, with the West Point Lighthouse in frame.
The group never toured until a 25th-anniversary run in 2016 — Cornell's last performances of the song before his death in 2017.

title: Let It Go
description: Elsa's ice-palace power ballad from Frozen — the song that rewrote its heroine from villain to misunderstood, won an Oscar, and lodged itself in every parent's head for a decade.

pops.text: The song was written by husband-and-wife team Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez for Disney's Frozen (2013).
Idina Menzel voices Elsa and sings it as Elsa builds her ice palace and embraces her powers.
Writing it changed the movie: once the Lopezes framed Elsa's anthem of self-acceptance, the character was rewritten from villain to sympathetic heroine.
It won the Academy Award for Best Original Song at the 2014 Oscars.
That Oscar night, John Travolta famously introduced Menzel as 'Adele Dazeem' — a flub she later turned into a running joke.
The song also won the Grammy for Best Song Written for Visual Media.
Menzel's film version reached No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 — remarkable for an animated-musical showstopper.
Demi Lovato recorded the pop single version that played over the end credits in many releases.
Frozen became the highest-grossing animated film of its era, and this was its signature number.
The Lopezes returned for Frozen II; Robert Lopez is an EGOT winner — one of the youngest ever to complete the set.

artist: Ziggy Marley and the Melody Makers
title: Look Who's Dancing
description: From One Bright Day, the Marley siblings' joyful roll call of unlikely dancers — grandmothers included — that carried the family band to a second straight Grammy and a US alternative-chart hit.

pops.text: The track is from One Bright Day, released in 1989 by Ziggy Marley and the Melody Makers.
Ziggy co-wrote it with his younger brother Stephen Marley, who was still a teenager at the time.
The Melody Makers were Bob Marley's children — Ziggy with siblings Sharon, Cedella and Stephen.
The group took its name from Melody Maker, the British music magazine.
One Bright Day won the Grammy for Best Reggae Album — the group's second consecutive win after Conscious Party.
The single was a crossover hit on US modern-rock radio, reaching No. 2 on Billboard's alternative chart.
The lyric works like a dance-floor roll call, spotting everyone from old 'Granny B' getting down to the dancers of the world.
The song's groove leans on dancehall and pop as much as roots reggae — the Melody Makers' late-80s signature blend.
The official video was newly restored and re-posted to Ziggy Marley's official YouTube channel.
Ziggy was 20 when the album came out — already a decade into performing, having formed the Melody Makers as a child in 1979.

title: American Girl
description: Recorded on the Fourth of July, 1976, the jangling closer of Petty's debut flopped as a single, then slowly became his signature — the very last song he ever played onstage.

pops.text: Tom Petty wrote it, and the band recorded it on July 4, 1976 — America's Bicentennial — a fitting birthday for the song.
It closes the band's self-titled debut album, released in November 1976 on Shelter Records.
Released as a single in February 1977, it failed to chart in the US at all.
The 12-string jangle channels The Byrds so faithfully that Roger McGuinn joked when he first heard it, he wondered when he'd recorded it.
McGuinn then covered the song himself on his 1977 solo album Thunderbyrd.
Petty always denied the persistent rumor that the lyric was about a suicide at the University of Florida in his hometown of Gainesville.
The song got a famous second life in The Silence of the Lambs (1991), sung along to in a car by a character driving toward danger.
It also turns up in Fast Times at Ridgemont High and Scrubs — a go-to needle-drop for restless youth.
Petty and the Heartbreakers played it at their 2002 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction.
It was the final song of Petty's final concert, at the Hollywood Bowl on September 25, 2017 — a week before his death.

title: Close to Me
description: A claustrophobic whisper of a single — Robert Smith breathing into the mic, the whole band stuffed into a wardrobe for the video — that nearly never made The Head on the Door at all.

pops.text: 'Close to Me' was the second single from The Head on the Door, released September 17, 1985.
Smith has said the song nearly didn't make the album — it was rescued with late production and lyric changes.
On its first release it reached No. 24 in the UK, No. 7 in Australia and No. 4 in Ireland.
The breathy, close-miked vocal and handclap rhythm make it one of the most intimate-sounding Cure singles.
Director Tim Pope filmed the video with the band crammed inside a wardrobe teetering on a cliff edge.
Smith himself suggested the wardrobe-on-a-cliff idea to match the song's uncomfortable, trapped feeling.
The video treatment fed back into the music — the band remixed the song denser and more claustrophobic for the clip.
In 1990 it was remixed again for the Mixed Up album, with an added brass section, and re-released as a single.
The 1990 remix outperformed the original in the UK, reaching No. 13, and scraped the US Hot 100 at No. 97.
The Head on the Door was The Cure's pop breakthrough album, recorded with the classic lineup including Porl Thompson and Boris Williams.

title: Goodbye Stranger
description: Rick Davies' Wurlitzer-driven farewell from Breakfast in America — a drifter's shrug of a song, answered in falsetto by Roger Hodgson, that became the album's second US hit single.

pops.text: It's a highlight of Breakfast in America, Supertramp's blockbuster album released March 29, 1979.
Rick Davies sings lead; as with all the band's songs, it's officially credited to Davies and Roger Hodgson jointly.
The album was nearly called Hello Stranger — the Davies and Hodgson songs were conceived as a dialogue between their opposing outlooks.
That dialogue is in the track itself: Davies' verses get answered by Hodgson's falsetto 'goodbye stranger' choruses.
Davies' Wurlitzer electric piano drives the groove from the very first bars.
Released as a single in mid-1979, it reached No. 15 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Breakfast in America topped the US album chart for six weeks and sold in the millions, making Supertramp unlikely superstars.
The song became a famous movie moment in Paul Thomas Anderson's Magnolia (1999), blasted and sung along to by the cast.
Guitarist John Helliwell's sax and the band's stacked harmonies fill out the long, looping outro.
Davies and Hodgson's creative split ended the classic partnership in 1983, when Hodgson left — making this early friction oddly prophetic.

title: With Plenty of Money and You
description: A 1936 Gold Diggers tune gets 90-proof Basie swing: Bennett, recorded on January 5, 1959 with the Count's orchestra and Ralph Sharon's arrangement, sounds like a man already spending it.

pops.text: Harry Warren and Al Dubin wrote the song for the film Gold Diggers of 1937, choreographed by Busby Berkeley.
Bennett recorded this version on January 5, 1959, with Count Basie and His Orchestra.
The arrangement is by Ralph Sharon, Bennett's longtime pianist and musical director.
It appears on Basie Swings, Bennett Sings, the Roulette Records half of their two-album collaboration.
Contract wrangling shaped the project: Bennett was Columbia's artist and Basie was Roulette's, so they made one album for each label — the Columbia set was In Person!.
The pairing was a dream for Bennett, a lifelong jazz fan who had long admired Basie's band.
The Basie orchestra of this era — the 'New Testament' band — was famed for its precision, blues-drenched swing.
The song itself is a Depression-era wish list: everything the singer could do, if only the money showed up.
Bennett's version enjoyed a second life on screen, turning up in the 2006 comedy Click's soundtrack.
Bennett was 32 at the session, still a decade from 'I Left My Heart in San Francisco' making him immortal.

title: Fire on the Bayou
description: The title track of the Meters' 1975 album is New Orleans funk at its greasiest — a call-and-response chant over a groove so deep that hip-hop producers spent decades mining this band's catalog.

pops.text: 'Fire on the Bayou' is the title track of The Meters' 1975 album on Reprise Records.
All five members share the writing credit: Art Neville, Cyril Neville, George Porter Jr., Joseph 'Zigaboo' Modeliste and Leo Nocentelli.
Cyril Neville had just joined his brother Art in the band, adding percussion and vocals for this album era.
The Meters were New Orleans' definitive funk band — and the house band for producer Allen Toussaint's sessions.
They backed Dr. John, Labelle and Robert Palmer, and played on Paul McCartney's Venus and Mars sessions in New Orleans.
Their records were cut at Toussaint and Marshall Sehorn's Sea-Saint Studio in New Orleans.
The track is built on a chant — 'fire on the bayou' answered by the band — over Modeliste's famously slippery drumming.
Modeliste's second-line rhythms became a foundational text for funk drummers and, later, hip-hop producers.
The Meters never had big pop hits — 'Cissy Strut' was their highest-charting single — yet their influence vastly outran their sales.
The original lineup's reunion shows in later decades opened with exactly this one-two spirit: 'Fire on the Bayou' into 'Cissy Strut'.
